answer: echo is a language construct, not a function: it outputs one or more strings. It takes no parentheses requirement and returns nothing. Use commas to output several values at once.
pitfall: echo is not a function, so echo('a','b') with two arguments in parentheses is a parse error. Use echo 'a', 'b'; or echo('a' . 'b');.
title: echo - output text (language construct, not a function)

answer: print is a language construct that outputs one string and always returns 1, so it can be used inside an expression. echo is faster and more common; print exists for expression contexts.
pitfall: print accepts only one argument. print 'a', 'b'; is a parse error.
title: print - output one string and return 1 (language construct)

answer: isset() returns true only if the variable exists and is not null. It never raises an undefined-variable notice, so it is the safe way to check optional input such as $_GET['page'] before reading it.
pitfall: isset() on a null value returns false. If null is a valid value for you, use array_key_exists() for arrays instead.
title: isset - check a variable exists and is not null

answer: empty() returns true for false, 0, 0.0, '', '0', null, an empty array, or an unset variable, and never raises a notice. Use it for 'is this field filled in?' checks, not for 'does this exist?' checks.
pitfall: empty('0') is true, so a form field containing the string '0' looks empty. For numeric input, check with isset() and a strict comparison instead.
title: empty - check a value is empty (0, '', null, false, [] or unset)

answer: unset() destroys a variable, an array element, or an object property. Unsetting an array element does not re-index the remaining keys; use array_values() afterwards if you need keys 0, 1, 2 again.
pitfall: After unset(), the array still has the old keys. A foreach over it skips the removed slot, but $marks[1] no longer exists.
title: unset - destroy a variable or array element

answer: include loads and runs another PHP file at that point. If the file is missing, PHP emits a warning and keeps running. Use it for optional parts such as a header or footer template.
pitfall: A missing include is only a warning, so a page can render half-broken. Use require for files the page cannot work without.
title: include - load another PHP file (warning if missing)

answer: include_once works like include, but if the same file was already included it is skipped. This prevents 'cannot redeclare function' errors when the same helper file is reached through several paths.
pitfall: include_once resolves the path each time, so the same file reached by two different relative paths can still load twice. Prefer one absolute base path.
title: include_once - include a file only once

answer: require loads and runs another PHP file. If the file is missing, PHP stops with a fatal error. Use it for files the script cannot work without, such as configuration or database bootstrap code.
pitfall: require stops the whole script on a missing file. For optional templates, use include instead.
title: require - load another PHP file (fatal error if missing)

answer: require_once works like require, but a file already loaded is skipped. It is the standard way to load class and function definition files exactly once.
pitfall: require_once is for definitions and bootstrap code. Do not use it for output templates that are meant to render more than once.
title: require_once - require a file only once

answer: list() assigns array values to variables in order. The modern short syntax [$a, $b] = $pair; does the same and is preferred in new code. Keys can be named in the short syntax.
pitfall: list() works on integer keys starting at 0 by default. For string keys, use the named form: ['name' => $name] = $row;.
title: list - unpack array values into variables

answer: eval() runs a string as PHP code. It exists for rare tooling cases such as template engines. It must never receive user input: injected code runs with the full permissions of the script.
pitfall: Never eval() data from a request, a file upload, or a database field. Prefer a data format, a callback, or a real parser instead.
title: eval - run a string as PHP code (dangerous, avoid user input)

answer: exit stops script execution immediately. With a string it prints the message first; with an integer it sets the process exit status (0 means success). Shutdown functions still run.
code:
<?php
$loggedIn = false;
if (!$loggedIn) {
    exit("Please log in first.");
}
echo "Welcome";
?>
pitfall: Code after exit() never runs. Do not put cleanup code after it; register a shutdown function or clean up before exiting.
title: exit - stop the script, optionally with a message or status

answer: die is exactly the same construct as exit: it stops the script, optionally printing a message. The two names are interchangeable; exit is the more common spelling in modern code.
code:
<?php
$data = file_get_contents('data.txt');
if ($data === false) {
    die("Could not read data.txt");
}
echo $data;
?>
pitfall: die() in the middle of a library function makes the caller's code untestable. Throw an exception instead and let the caller decide.
title: die - alias of exit (language construct)

answer: declare sets a directive for the file. declare(strict_types=1); must be the first statement in the file and makes scalar type checks strict for calls made from that file. Without it, PHP coerces '5' to int 5.
code:
<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function doubleIt(int $n): int
{
    return $n * 2;
}
echo doubleIt(21);
?>
pitfall: declare(strict_types=1) must be the very first statement, before any other code or output, or it is a fatal error.
title: declare - set a directive for a file, e.g. strict_types

answer: clone makes a shallow copy of an object: scalar properties are copied, but nested objects are still shared. Define __clone() in the class to deep-copy nested objects when independence is required.
code:
<?php
class Box
{
    public int $count = 1;
}
$a = new Box();
$b = clone $a;
$b->count = 9;
echo $a->count . '-' . $b->count;
?>
pitfall: clone is shallow. If the object holds another object, changing it through the clone changes the original too, unless __clone() copies it.
title: clone - shallow copy of an object

answer: instanceof checks whether an object is an instance of a class, a subclass, or an implementation of an interface. It returns false for non-objects instead of raising an error.
code:
<?php
class Animal {}
class Dog extends Animal {}
$dog = new Dog();
var_dump($dog instanceof Dog);
var_dump($dog instanceof Animal);
var_dump($dog instanceof stdClass);
?>
pitfall: instanceof with a string class name checks the variable against that name. If the class does not exist, it simply returns false.
title: instanceof - check an object is of a class or interface

answer: new creates an object and runs the class constructor with the given arguments. Since PHP 8, new can appear inside an expression, for example new DateTime()->format('Y').
code:
<?php
class User
{
    public function __construct(public string $name) {}
}
$user = new User('Prabh');
echo $user->name;
?>
pitfall: new with a class name held in a variable, new $className(), fails at runtime if the class does not exist. Check class_exists() for dynamic names.
title: new - create an object from a class

answer: throw raises an exception object. Since PHP 8 it is an expression, so it can appear in arrow functions, the null coalescing operator, and match arms. Uncaught exceptions stop the script, so throw only where the caller can catch it.
code:
<?php
function getAge(int $age): int
{
    if ($age < 0) {
        throw new InvalidArgumentException('Age cannot be negative');
    }
    return $age;
}
try {
    echo getAge(-1);
} catch (InvalidArgumentException $e) {
    echo 'Caught: ' . $e->getMessage();
}
?>
pitfall: throw new Exception('msg') without a try/catch anywhere is an uncaught exception and a fatal error in effect. Catch at a boundary that can report or recover.
title: throw - raise an exception (also an expression in PHP 8)

answer: yield turns a function into a generator: values are produced one at a time, only when the caller asks for the next one. This keeps memory flat when looping over large sets, because the whole list is never built at once.
code:
<?php
function countUp(int $n): iterable
{
    for ($i = 1; $i <= $n; $i++) {
        yield $i;
    }
}
foreach (countUp(3) as $v) {
    echo $v;
}
?>
pitfall: A generator function returns nothing when called; its body does not run until the first foreach/next. Calling it and expecting immediate side effects is a common surprise.
title: yield - return a value from a generator, lazily

answer: yield from delegates to another generator, array, or Traversable, yielding all of its values (and its keys) in order. It is how generators are composed without manual loops.
code:
<?php
function inner(): iterable
{
    yield 'a';
    yield 'b';
}
function outer(): iterable
{
    yield from inner();
    yield 'c';
}
foreach (outer() as $v) {
    echo $v;
}
?>
pitfall: yield from with integer keys re-indexes them in the outer generator. Preserve string keys explicitly if key identity matters.
title: yield from - delegate to another generator or iterable

answer: match is an expression that returns a value. It compares with strict identity (===), so '1' does not match 1, and it throws UnhandledMatchError when no arm matches and no default is given. It is not a function and not a statement like switch.
pitfall: match uses ===. A string '2' will not match the integer arm 2 and falls through to default or throws. Cast the subject first when the type is uncertain.
title: match - strict comparison expression returning a value (PHP 8)

answer: fn($x) => $x * 2; is an arrow function: a one-expression closure that automatically captures surrounding variables by value. It cannot contain statements, and captured variables cannot be modified through it.
pitfall: Arrow functions capture by value at creation time. Changing $factor afterwards does not change what the arrow function sees.
title: fn - arrow function, auto-captures variables by value

answer: A static variable inside a function is initialised once and keeps its value between calls to that function. It is per-function state, not shared with other functions or with the outside scope.
code:
<?php
function counter(): int
{
    static $n = 0;
    $n++;
    return $n;
}
echo counter() . counter() . counter();
?>
pitfall: A static variable cannot be reset from outside the function. If the count must be resettable, use a class property or pass the state explicitly.
title: static variable - a local variable that keeps its value between calls
